title: Dead of Night
review: 1940s British screenwriting acting is very different to what we're used to now. It's very presentational, rather than naturalistic. It takes a few moments to become attuned to it whenever I watch old movies, but after a while some surprisingly good performances emerge. There's an impressive ghost child actor in this who looks like aren't any older than seven. This is an anthology of ghost stories, where the story itself is intended to be the source of horror, rather than any direct depictions of tension or suffering. For example, you will see a man telling the story of a another man who cut his own throat, rather than seeing the act take place itself. As a result it's not particularly shocking to someone who has already seen {Evil Dead II}, while that film would fry the brain of someone in the 1940s. Think about how much our sensibilities changed in that 40 year gap, though the power of film.
spoilers: There's a comedy story half way through about an incompetent ghost, that's a bit like {It's a Wonderful Life}. This might be the best ending of any horror anthology I've seen.
